query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled annealing followed by rapid quenching treatment in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs induces the formation of fine, coherent precipitates within a predominantly FCC matrix, which in turn stabilizes the phase over a wide temperature range and supports high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with a primarily FCC structure and uniform element distribution.
generation.intervention: Apply a precise heat/thermomechanical treatment consisting of annealing at an elevated temperature to promote nanoscale precipitate nucleation, followed by rapid quenching to preserve their coherence within the FCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Conduct controlled tests at high temperatures (using mechanical strength, oxidation, and irradiation evaluations) and at cryogenic temperatures (via tensile and impact testing) while comparing samples processed with rapid quenching to baseline samples that are slowly cooled after similar annealing.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent precipitates (e.g., L12 or B2 phases) formed within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The coherent precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion and inhibit unwanted phase transformations by stabilizing the FCC matrix. This microstructural control reduces defect accumulation and supports multiple performance criteria across temperature extremes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to slowly cooled samples, alloys subjected to the controlled annealing and quenching process will exhibit more refined and coherent precipitates, resulting in enhanced phase stability. This leads to improved high-temperature strength, better oxidation and radiation resistance, and increased toughness at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.baseline: Samples processed by similar annealing but with slow cooling, expected to form coarser or incoherent precipitates associated with less stable phase distributions and inferior mechanical and environmental performance.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni composition system under the specific controlled heat and quenching treatments described. Deviations in composition or processing parameters might result in different precipitate characteristics and thereby limit the generality of the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: While prior related studies support the role of coherent precipitates in stabilizing phases, the precise nature, size, and distribution of the precipitates and their quantitative effects on properties across varying environments remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples: one set receives the controlled annealing plus rapid quenching treatment while the control set is allowed to cool slowly after annealing. Characterize the microstructures using TEM and EBSD to compare precipitate size, distribution, and coherence. Then, evaluate mechanical properties (tensile strength, impact toughness) at both high-temperature and cryogenic conditions, alongside oxidation and radiation exposure tests.
measurements: Precipitate size, distribution, and coherence (via TEM/EBSD)
Mechanical performance at high and cryogenic temperatures (tensile strength, ductility, impact toughness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly quenched samples do not exhibit significantly finer and more coherent precipitates compared to the slowly cooled samples, or if there is no measurable improvement in phase stability and associated mechanical/environmental properties, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Furthermore, they show that sample B exhibits a smaller grain size compared to sample E or F, presenting average values of 2.9 µm, 10.7 µm, and 13.5 µm, respectively. It is important to note that the diffraction patterns of the ordered and disordered BCC phases are very similar, making it difficult to distinguish them by EBSD. However, the presence in sample E of a Cr and Fe-rich phase and an Al and Ni-rich phase, corresponding to disordered and ordered BCC structures, respectively, is confirmed by EDS (regions 2 and 1 in Figure 10 and Figure 11). The phase transformations of the Ni36Co18Cr20Fe19Al7 HEA have been studied in this research paper. The alloy underwent hot forging, cold rolling, annealing at and quenching from 1323 K, and isothermal holding, at 873 K. The as-quenched HEA is a single FCC. After the 873-K isothermal holding, the coherent fine L12 particles precipitated homogeneously in the FCC matrix. In addition, cellular precipitation occurred, resulting in the transformation of the high-temperature FCC phase into lamellae of the low-temperature FCC phase and L12 phase. The colonies nucleated and grew from the grain boundaries. The grain boundary moved with the growing tips of the newly formed lamellar FCC and L12 phases, and the lamellar FCC grains had the same orientation as that of one neighboring FCC grain and grew into the other neighboring FCC grain, with a different orientation. The lamellar L12 grains had the following composition: Ni60Co8Cr6Fe6Al20, and the FCC grains had the following composition: Ni31Co15Cr28Fe21Al4. The lamellar L12 phase was rich in Ni and Al, and lean in Co, Cr, and Fe, and the lamellar FCC phase was contrary to this.

reading.lever: Use controlled annealing and quenching to induce coherent precipitate formation in the FCC matrix, thereby tailoring phase stability across temperature extremes.
reading.why: This combined processing approach, previously successful in related HEAs, directly manipulates microstructural evolution to govern phase stability and meet multi-environment performance criteria.
